planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; established clumps can also be divided in spring or fall.

directions: Grolau is a German-bred chive selection prized for unusually broad, thick, dark green foliage that stays tender even as clumps mature, making it a favorite for continuous cutting and for forcing indoors during winter months. Divide congested clumps every two to three years to keep leaf production vigorous and to prevent the center from thinning out. The plant sends up abundant lilac-pink flower heads in late spring, which pollinators favor and which can be removed to redirect energy into leaf growth. Because the leaves are noticeably thicker than standard chives, Grolau holds up well to freezing or drying for winter storage.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring, or start a fall crop in midsummer; hilling soil around the base as stems lengthen produces the long blanched shanks traditional for negi.

directions: Nabechan is a traditional Japanese negi-type bunching onion grown for its long, thick, upright white shanks that resist splitting and curling even in hot weather. Sow into a shallow furrow and gradually mound soil around the base every few weeks as the plants grow, which blanches the lower stalk into the long white shaft prized for hot pot dishes. The sweet, mild flavor and non-bulbing habit make it equally useful sliced raw as a garnish or cooked whole in soups and nabemono. It tolerates both summer heat and winter cold well, allowing extended harvest windows in most temperate gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring for summer harvest or in late summer for a cold-hardy overwintering crop; Kincho is bred to hold in the field through cold snaps without bolting.

directions: Kincho is a Japanese non-bulbing bunching onion bred for reliable cold hardiness and improved resistance to pink root and botrytis leaf blight compared to older heirloom types. It forms upright, uniform stalks well suited to late-season and overwintered plantings where other bunching onions struggle. Sow thickly and thin gradually, harvesting outer plants first while allowing remaining stalks room to thicken. Its disease tolerance and cold resilience make it a dependable choice for extending green onion harvests into fall and winter in temperate climates.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring several weeks before last frost; dill does not transplant well, so sow in place and succession sow every 3-4 weeks for continuous leaf harvest.

directions: Delikat is a European leaf-type dill selected for dense, bushy growth and heavy foliage yield rather than for seed production, making it a good choice for gardeners who mainly want fresh dill weed. Its compact stature compared to tall seed-strain dills also suits container growing and small raised beds. Harvest leaves regularly by snipping outer stems, which encourages the bushy plant to keep pushing new growth before it eventually bolts to flower. Like other dill, it self-sows readily if a few plants are allowed to set seed, and its ferny foliage supports black swallowtail butterfly caterpillars.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Selma Fino is bred for reliable bulbing without premature bolting.

directions: Selma Fino is an Italian Florence fennel cultivar selected for large, heavy, uniform white bulbs and strong resistance to bolting when sown in cool spring conditions. Sow directly and thin seedlings so bulbs have room to swell, then hill soil around the base as the bulb develops to keep it blanched, tender, and mild. Its sweet, pronounced anise flavor makes it popular for both raw and cooked preparations, and it holds in the garden longer than many older bulbing strains before splitting or flowering. A fall sowing timed to mature in cool autumn weather often produces the largest, most tender bulbs.

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; soak seed overnight to help speed the naturally slow germination.

directions: Krausa is a German curly-leaf parsley selection known for exceptionally dense, tightly ruffled triple-curled leaves on strong, upright stalks that hold their bright to medium green color well through summer heat. It is notably vigorous and heavy-yielding compared to older curly types, giving multiple cuttings from a single planting. As a biennial it overwinters in mild climates and can be harvested through winter before it flowers and sets seed the following year. Its dense, crisp foliage keeps its texture well after cutting, making it useful both as a fresh garnish and for drying.
